iut_type: End Product (Ricoh Imaging camera) referencing a third-party RF module (Murata LBEE5PL2DL Type 2DL) for RF/RF PHY/LL, Power Class registration mismatch dispute
customer_question: Our product's measured RF PHY output power result is Class 2 level, but the module's registered reference QDID (Q302534) is registered as Power Class 1 'Support: YES.' Since our product's reference QDID is registered as Class 1 but our test result is Class 2, we can't Include/reference that QDID for our registration. Can the module manufacturer provide (or create) a QDID/DN registered with Power Class 1 set to 'Support: NO' so we can properly reference a Class-2-only registration? Separately — given Japan's Radio Law construction-design certification for this module caps the legal output power well below the Class 1 (>10mW) threshold, isn't the module's Class 1: YES Bluetooth SIG registration itself a legally problematic/erroneous registration? And once that's resolved: must our registration always match the module/IC's registered Power Class exactly, or can we just run our own full RF PHY test to Pass at our actual (lower) output level instead of referencing the module's registration at all?
question_variants: Does the module manufacturer have an obligation to register a Class-2-only (Power Class 1: NO) QDID for our use, since our actual measured output doesn't reach Class 1?
If the module's purchase/delivery specification document specifies Class 2 (not Class 1) output power, is the module manufacturer obligated to provide a matching Class 2-only module registration?

Since Japan's Radio Law construction-design certification number for this module caps output power below the Class 1 threshold (>10mW), and the module's BT SIG registration is Class 1: YES, is that SIG registration itself invalid/erroneous and must it be corrected?

If we drop Power Class 1 support during registration (uncheck Power Class 1 in RFPHY and LL), we're told we then need to submit our own RFPHY and the IC vendor's LL test reports as evidence — is that correct, and can the module manufacturer instead just provide those reports?
Why does our product's actual output power differ so much from the module vendor's own registered/datasheet TxPower in the first place?
Must our registration's declared Power Class always match the module/IC's registered Power Class exactly, or can we just test and Pass at our own actual (lower) output level instead?
If we can't reference the module's registration directly, can we instead just run our own full RF PHY test at our real settings to Pass independently?
Is it acceptable for our SIG registration to show 'Class 1' on paper while our product never actually transmits above our own much lower per-country regulatory ceiling?
actual_issue: The customer's actual RF PHY test result on their finished product was Class 2-level output power, but the only available module reference QDID was registered as Power Class 1 ('Support: YES'), creating an ICS mismatch that blocked referencing (Include) that QDID for the customer's own SIG registration. The customer escalated by gathering objective evidence (Japan Radio Law construction-design certification limiting legal output power to a Class 1.5-equivalent level, and a Class 1.5 power class explicitly stated in the module's own datasheet alongside a separate, seemingly contradictory 'Output Power setting = 13dBm' figure) to argue the module's Class 1: YES SIG registration was itself erroneous, and pushed the module manufacturer to either register a Class-2-only QDID or correct the existing one. The module manufacturer repeatedly resisted, reiterating that a Class-2-only registration would be a paid, lead-time service. The deadlock was resolved in stages: first by clarifying that Bluetooth SIG registration and national radio-law certification are independent compliance regimes; then, once a more senior customer contact (Daigo Kenji) explained the actual underlying engineering reason for the power mismatch, by confirming that a SIG-registered Power Class is a maximum-capability ceiling rather than a floor, and that a critical technical obstacle (introduced by the July 2024 registration system change) made resolving the ICS mismatch by modifying the registration itself practically infeasible for a set-maker without IC-level source access.
plain_english_explanation:
Several distinct threads converged in this dispute. First, on legal/regulatory grounds: Bluetooth SIG's Power Class declaration and each country's radio-law output power limits are evaluated independently. The module's Class 1: YES SIG registration is not erroneous merely because the customer's product, as actually configured, transmits lower — the module remains technically capable of Class 1 operation under different firmware/regional configuration, which is exactly what the SIG registration declares.

Second, on why the customer's actual output differs from the module vendor's own datasheet/regulatory-approval TxPower in the first place: a more senior customer contact explained that since this camera model is manufactured by an outsourced production partner, Ricoh has no direct delivery-specification agreement with the module vendor. The vendor's datasheet TxPower reflects power levels the vendor itself evaluated and used to obtain its own per-country radio approvals — but that power level is too high for a digital camera to use, since it would fail SAR (Specific Absorption Rate, a human radiation-exposure safety limit) testing. Separately, this camera's module variant has no antenna attached (an antenna-less module type), and the antenna the vendor used for its own per-country radio approvals is physically too large to fit in a camera. For both reasons, Ricoh independently sets its own (lower) TxPower and obtains its own separate per-country radio approvals at that lower level — a practice the module vendor is aware of and has accepted for this and prior camera models.

Third, on whether the registration must therefore match the module's registered Class exactly: it does not. A SIG-registered Output Power level represents a maximum capability ceiling, not a floor — a product is free to implement and ship at any actual Output Power at or below that ceiling without any registration change required, and without needing to alter per-country radio-law approvals, as long as the actual implementation never exceeds whatever ceiling those separate per-country approvals already specify.

Fourth, and most technically significant: the customer asked whether, instead of referencing the module's (mismatched) registration at all, they could simply run their own full RF PHY test at their actual settings and register independently. This turned out to be specifically blocked by a change introduced with the registration system update effective July 1, 2024: cross-layer (inter-layer) consistency checking was strengthened, such that referencing the module's QDID while uploading the customer's own RF PHY test report (showing a non-Class-1 result) would trigger an Invalid against the separately-registered [LL] (Link Layer) item's 'LE Power Class 1: YES' declaration. Avoiding that Invalid by changing the ICS declaration would, under the new system, now require testing every single LL-layer test item — and because a set-maker like Ricoh treats the IC/chipset layer as a black box (no source code or internal test access), any LL-layer item that came back Fail could not be diagnosed or fixed, making ICS-based resolution of the inter-layer mismatch practically impossible for a set-maker in this position, regardless of cost.

Given all of this, the practical resolution proposed and accepted was: proceed with the customer's registration referencing the module's existing QDID exactly as registered (showing RF PHY: Class 1 'on paper'), since the customer confirmed their actual per-country radio-law ceiling (a maximum of approximately +3dBm in their case) would never be exceeded by their real implementation regardless of what the SIG registration shows, and no change to any existing per-country radio approval was required. As a parallel, low-probability-of-success effort, the consultant still recommended sending the module manufacturer one more email citing the strongest available evidence (the Japan radio-law construction-design certification value and the datasheet both showing Class 1.5, closely matching the customer's actual ceiling) as decisive proof the Class 1 registration was technically incorrect — while noting from past experience that this particular module manufacturer has a track record of never reversing a stated position even when shown to be wrong, so this was attempted mainly to leave no avenue unexplored rather than out of genuine expectation of success.
consultant_answer: On the legal question: Bluetooth SIG registration and each country's radio-law output power rules are independent compliance regimes — the module's Class 1: YES SIG registration isn't erroneous just because your product transmits lower; the module is still technically capable of Class 1 under other regional configurations, which is exactly what the registration declares. On why your actual power differs from the vendor's datasheet: that's a SAR-compliance and antenna-size constraint specific to your camera design, not a registration error — and the vendor is aware you set your own lower power independently. On whether your registration must match the module's Class exactly: no — a SIG-registered Power Class is a maximum ceiling, not a floor; you can ship at any actual power at or below it with no registration change needed, as long as you never exceed your own per-country radio-law approvals (which you've confirmed you won't). On running your own full RF PHY test to register independently instead of referencing the module: unfortunately, the registration system's strengthened inter-layer consistency check (effective since July 2024) would flag an Invalid against the module's separately-registered LL Power Class 1:YES declaration, and fixing that via an ICS change would now require testing every LL item — which isn't practically possible for you as a set-maker without IC-level source access if any of those came back Fail. Given that, we'd recommend proceeding with your registration referencing the module's existing QDID and ICS exactly as-is (Class 1 on paper), since your actual implementation will never exceed your own confirmed lower ceiling either way. We'll still send the module manufacturer one more email with the strongest evidence as a long shot, but past experience suggests they're unlikely to change their registered Class regardless.
decision_logic: Bluetooth SIG Power Class registration and a country's national radio-law output power ceiling are evaluated independently, and a SIG-registered Power Class represents a maximum capability ceiling rather than a floor — a product may ship at any actual output power at or below that ceiling without any registration change, as long as it stays within its own separately-obtained per-country radio approvals. When a set-maker's actual test result doesn't match a referenced module's registered Class, attempting to resolve the mismatch by changing the ICS declaration (rather than accepting the existing registration or pursuing a true Class-2-only reference) must be evaluated against the current registration system's inter-layer consistency rules: under the post-July-2024 system, an ICS change to avoid a cross-layer Invalid can cascade into requiring full retesting of every item in the affected layer, which is infeasible for a set-maker without source-level access to a black-box IC/chipset layer — making 'just register independently with our own test results' a viable-sounding but ultimately blocked option in this specific registration-system era.
final_recommendation: When a customer disputes a referenced module's registered Power Class based on their own measured results, first separate the legal/regulatory question (SIG registration vs. national radio law are independent, and SIG Power Class is a ceiling not a floor) from the practical registration-mechanics question (whether an ICS change, a new lower-class reference, or accepting the existing mismatched-but-valid reference is the actual path forward) — and when a set-maker proposes testing and registering independently instead of referencing an upstream module/IC registration, explicitly check whether the current registration system's inter-layer consistency rules would require full retesting of a black-box layer the set-maker cannot access, since that can silently foreclose what otherwise looks like the cleanest solution.
risk_if_done_wrong: Treating a module's broader SIG Power Class declaration as legally invalid based on one country's narrower radio-law output ceiling could lead to an unproductive, prolonged dispute with the module manufacturer; separately, encouraging a set-maker to pursue independent full-test registration without first checking the inter-layer consistency requirements of the current registration system could lead them into a dead end where an IC-layer test item fails and cannot be diagnosed or fixed, since they lack source-level access to that layer.
